newsitem.title: UK: Abortion politics land in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Abortion politics land in Britain.

text.p: Abortion politics hit Britain on Thursday when the Pro-Life Alliance promised to fight all out at the next election even as it condemned the violent U.S. campaign against a woman's right to choose.

The party unveiled a manifesto outlining "absolute respect for innocent human life from fertilisation until natural death" and promised to field 50 to 70 candidates against pro-choice members of the major political parties.

"We face in this country now a great disrespect for human life," Bruno Quintavalle, director of the alliance, told a news conference. "The parties just choose to ignore these very grave issues. Within this vacuum, we felt it was very important to stand up as a witness to the truth of this cause."

Unlike in the United States and many Catholic countries in Europe, abortion has traditionally been a political sideline in Britain, where members of parliament are largely left to vote with their conscience rather than toe a party line.

What is more, single-issue parties tend to garner little support in Britain, witnessed by the Referendum Party's expensive effort to enter the mainstream by threatening to field candidates against anyone at odds with its stance on Europe.
The privately-funded pro-life alliance would not say which politicians it would target but distributed a long list of pro-choice candidates, many of them top members of the opposition Labour Party.
Its stated aim: to outlaw all abortion in Britain unless the mother's life is at risk, restrict some aspects of assisted conception and ban all forms of euthanasia.
The group hoped to run a party political broadcast before the election, which must be held by May 22, and refused to rule out using graphic footage of an abortion to make its point.
While 50 candidates entitles a party to national air time, it is far from sure the party would win the right to screen such images, nor that shock tactics would win it support.

Indeed, the party was quick to distance itself from the confrontation that has shaped the U.S. debate, where picketing has escalated into murder. Well-organised Christian groups have forced their agenda into Republican politics and many supporters of choice have seen their message submerged by the moral right.
Britain was ripe for an anti-abortion campaign, Quintaville said, pointing to an ever-rising number of moral conundrums posed by scientists' growing ability to shape reproduction.
On Thursday, a British widow won the right to have a baby using her dead husband's sperm after a long legal fight. While she proclaimed victory, the treatment must take place abroad.

Her high-profile case followed an outcry over another woman's decision to abort one of her twins and a couple's decision to ignore medical advice for selective abortion and witness the death of eight foetuses following fertility treatment.
Pro-choice campaigners dismissed their opposition's foray into national politics as a publicity stunt doomed to fail.

"Their decision to stand in the election is driven by their desperation to break out...and become mainstream. While the PLA may attract a lot of attention, their views will remain those of a minority," said David Nolan of the Birth Control Trust.
